standard_prerequisites.name: The elementary divisor property for a 1 x 2 matrix over R
standard_prerequisites.use: Produces the invertible u and the invertible V that reduce (a b) to (f 0) and hence generate the equality (a, b) = (f).

standard_prerequisites.name: Invertibility of V implying that its first row generates the unit ideal
standard_prerequisites.use: Supplies (g_11, g_21) = R, which together with f = u a g_11 + u b g_21 gives the reverse inclusion.

core_obligations: For nonzero a, b in R consider the 1 x 2 matrix (a b) and apply the elementary divisor property to obtain an invertible u in R and an invertible 2 x 2 matrix V = (g_ij) with u(a b)V = (f 0) (proof lines 37825-37827).
Read off from that identity that f = u a g_11 + u b g_21, so f lies in the ideal (a, b), and that (g_11, g_21) = R because V is invertible (proof line 37828).
Combine the two to conclude (a, b) = (f), i.e. the ideal generated by two elements is principal (proof lines 37828-37829).
Pass from two generators to an arbitrary finitely generated ideal; the author states that this induction argument is omitted (proof line 37829).
difficulty_reason: The statement is a one-line implication: an elementary divisor domain is Bezout (source lines 37819-37822). The proof applies the elementary divisor property to the 1 x 2 matrix (a b), obtaining an invertible u and an invertible 2 x 2 matrix V with u(a b)V = (f 0), and then reads off both that f is a combination of a and b and that the pair (g_11, g_21) generates the unit ideal, because V is invertible (proof lines 37824-37828). The pair of conclusions is what forces (a, b) = (f). The author then invokes an induction on the number of generators to pass from two elements to an arbitrary finitely generated ideal and explicitly states that induction is omitted (proof line 37829), so that step is left to the reader.
